segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to the other side of the sea, to the region of the Gerasenes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he got out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He made his home among the tombs, and no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he had torn the chains apart and broken the shackles in pieces, and no one was strong enough to subdue him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Constantly, night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he was crying out and gashing himself with stones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and bowed down before him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and crying out in a loud voice he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you have to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I charge you by God, do not torment me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he had been saying to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he asked him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is your name?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My name is Legion, for we are many.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they begged him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand of them, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and were drowned in the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had been tending them fled and reported it in the town and in the countryside, and people came to see what it was that had happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind—the very man who had had the legion—and they were afraid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had seen it told them what had happened to the demon-possessed man, and about the pigs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they began to beg him to leave their territory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged him that he might be with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he did not let him. Instead he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go home to your own people and report to them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone was amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the synagogue leaders, named Jairus, came, and when he saw him he fell at his feet

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and begged him earnestly, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he went with him. A large crowd was following him and pressing in on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had endured much under many doctors and had spent everything she had, yet she was not helped at all but instead grew worse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When she heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for she said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If I touch even his clothes, I will be made well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately the source of her bleeding dried up, and she knew in her body that she had been healed of her affliction.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately Jesus, aware in himself that power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who touched my clothes?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You see the crowd pressing in on you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he kept looking around to see the woman who had done this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman, fearful and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be healthy, free of your affliction.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, ignoring what was being said, told the synagogue leader,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid; only believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he allowed no one to follow along with him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to the house of the synagogue leader, and he saw a commotion, with people weeping and wailing loudly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went in and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child has not died but is sleeping.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they laughed at him. But he put them all out, took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him, and went in where the child was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking the child by the hand, he said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Talitha koum,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which is translated,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Little girl, I say to you, get up.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately the little girl stood up and began to walk around, for she was twelve years old. And immediately they were overcome with great astonishment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gave them strict orders that no one should know of this, and told them to give her something to eat.

notes.note: Manuscripts vary among “Gerasenes,” “Gadarenes,” and “Gergesenes,” here and in the parallel passages. “Gerasenes” has the strongest early support in Mark, though the city of Gerasa lay more than thirty miles from the lake, which probably prompted the other readings. The KJV, following later manuscripts, has “Gadarenes.”

The Greek verb names the act of prostrating oneself in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it. The KJV has “worshipped” here; most modern versions use “bowed down” or “knelt before,” since the possessed man is acknowledging a superior power and pleading, not offering worship in the modern sense. The spirit’s address to Jesus as Son of the Most High God follows in the next verse.

The verb means to put someone under a solemn oath, and it was a regular term in ancient exorcism, where the exorcist adjures a spirit by a divine name (compare Acts 19:13). Here the roles are reversed: the possessed man turns the exorcist’s formula on Jesus.

A Latin military term taken over into Greek. A legion was the main unit of the Roman army, numbering roughly five thousand soldiers at full strength, so the name signals an overwhelming number. Some interpreters also hear an allusion to Roman occupation; that is possible but disputed.

Pigs were unclean animals under the Law of Moses (Leviticus 11:7) and were not kept by observant Jews. A large herd signals to the reader that the scene is set in largely Gentile territory, the region of the Decapolis east of the lake.

“The Lord” here most naturally refers to God, as in the Greek Scriptures, but the word could also be heard as referring to Jesus. In the next verse the man proclaims how much Jesus had done for him, and Mark may intend the reader to notice the overlap.

The phrase echoes the Greek of Leviticus 15:25–27, where a woman with a prolonged discharge of blood is ritually unclean, as is whatever she touches. Mark does not mention impurity directly, and scholars differ on how much weight it carries in the story.

The Greek verb, also used in verses 23 and 28, means to rescue or deliver, and covers both healing from illness and salvation in the fuller religious sense; it can equally be translated “has saved you.” The context here is physical healing, so “made well” is used, but a first-century reader would have heard the same word that elsewhere is rendered “save.”

The Greek verb can mean either “overhear” or “disregard.” Most recent versions choose “overhearing,” and Luke’s parallel has simply “hearing.” In the Septuagint and at Matthew 18:17, the only other New Testament passage where it occurs, it means to disregard or refuse to listen, so “ignoring” is used here; either reading is defensible.

These words are Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus and of Galilee, which Mark preserves and then translates for his Greek-speaking readers. Some manuscripts read “koumi,” the grammatically feminine form of the command, which is the reading the KJV follows.

candidates.reason: In healing stories translators split between “heal,” “make well,” and “save,” and the choice determines whether readers can see the link to the word’s salvation sense elsewhere.

Ranges across beg, urge, exhort, encourage, and comfort throughout the New Testament; the petition sense in the Gospels needs one fixed rendering so repeated uses like the five in this chapter stay visible.
Versions vary among “demon-possessed,” “demonized,” and “had a demon,” and “possession” is an interpretive English category the Greek verb does not itself spell out.
Mark’s signature adverb occurs dozens of times and is rendered variously as “immediately,” “at once,” “straightaway,” or dropped; a single decision preserves his style across chapters.
Used of the Sea of Galilee, which is a freshwater lake; some versions render “lake,” and the choice should be uniform across the Gospels.
